name: Frida Kahlo Museum
label: Frida Kahlo Museum
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Londres y Allende' (4 web pages); placed at crossing of Londres and Allende (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/176482295: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Frida Kahlo Museum' (53 m across).
notes: The blue house where Frida Kahlo lived, in Coyoacán.

text.description:
The Frida Kahlo Museum, better known as La Casa Azul (the Blue House), is the cobalt-blue house in Coyoacán where the artist was born, grew up and later died. It was built in 1904 and has since been simplified to the plainer facade you see today. Diego Rivera gave the house and its contents to be turned into a museum in her honour, and it has been open as one since 1958. It is among the most visited museums in Mexico City, with around 25,000 visitors a month, so expect company. The house is built around a central courtyard garden, but from the street you see only the strong blue walls.

It photographs well because the colours do the work for you. The deep blue is set off by red trim, green barred windows and a large tree overhanging the street, and the corner position lets you show two walls at once. The best view is from the corner of Londres and Allende, where the full facade fits in one frame. If the entrance is busy, Calle Allende gives a calmer view of the blue wall from the side. Weekday mornings are quieter than weekends and holidays, when the queue at the entrance can be long. Keep your phone level so the vertical lines stay straight, and leave a little pavement and sky in the frame so the house does not look cramped.
text.geographic_location: The museum is in Colonia del Carmen, in the Coyoacán borough of Mexico City. It stands on the corner of Londres and Allende streets.
text.directions_text: Head for Coyoacán and the Colonia del Carmen area and ask for the corner of Londres and Allende. The house itself is just to the north, about 30 m away. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole corner facade. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the pavement is narrow or you want to include the tree and the sky. Use 2x if you want a closer shot of the windows and trim without stepping into the road.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of Londres and Allende (corner of the cobalt facade facing the Londres and Allende junction). The full cobalt-blue corner facade of Casa Azul with red trim, green barred windows and a large tree above the street.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the corner of the house up with one vertical line so the walls stay straight. Keep the tree at the top of the frame and leave a little pavement at the bottom. For a quieter alternative with fewer people in the shot, walk along Calle Allende and photograph the blue wall from the side.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the blue wall to focus, then slide the exposure down a touch so the blue stays rich and the sky does not wash out. Try a Live Photo if people are passing, so you can pick the best moment afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon, roughly 3:30 to 5:00 pm, should give side light on the facade, but check it on the day. Weekday mornings are calmer for crowds, though the entrance side may be in shade.

text.access_note: The outside of the house can be photographed from the public street, but the museum itself is ticketed and has its own rules on interior photos, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Late afternoon, roughly 3:30 to 5:00 pm, gives side light on the corner facade, while mornings may leave the entrance in shade (to be verified on the ground).
Weekday mornings are calmer than weekends and holidays, when the entrance queue is long.
The corner of Londres and Allende is a public street where you can photograph the exterior without a museum ticket.
Calle Allende is usually less crowded than the main entrance.

name: Plaza Garibaldi
label: Plaza Garibaldi
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Mercado San Camilito' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Mercado San Camilito' (way/217662063): middle (183 m across); moved 15 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/15985584: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Plaza Garibaldi' (158 m across).

text.description: From there the nine large letters spelling GARIBALDI sit beside the maguey plant, with mariachi groups and other performers usually in the frame, so the sign, the people and the atmosphere all read at once. It is the postcard view of the square. The plaza was called Plaza Santa Cecilia until 1920, when it was renamed after Lt. Col. Peppino Garibaldi, who fought in the Mexican Revolution. Mariachi players have gathered here since the 1920s, when the Salón Tenampa, still on the north side of the square, became the place to hear them. The square was remodelled after 2009, so older photos with the kiosk no longer match what you will see. Keep your shot simple: let the letters fill the lower or middle of the frame and leave room above for the buildings and sky. For a different angle, the patio at the Museo del Tequila y el Mezcal looks over the square from slightly below street level, though you may need museum access, so check the official site before you go. If you ask musicians to pose, some may expect a small tip. Keep an eye on your phone and bag while you shoot.
text.geographic_location: Plaza Garibaldi is in the historic centre of Mexico City, on Eje Central (Lázaro Cárdenas), a few blocks north of the Palacio de Bellas Artes.
text.directions_text: Head for the Palacio de Bellas Artes and then go a few blocks north along Eje Central to reach the square, or take a taxi straight to Plaza Garibaldi. The middle of the square is to the south of this spot, about 2 minutes on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the letters with the performers behind. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close to the letters and want the whole sign and the market front in one frame. Use 2x telephoto, if your phone has it, for musicians at a distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Mercado San Camilito (in front of the market, beside the large GARIBALDI letters). The nine large letters spelling GARIBALDI with the maguey, mariachi groups and performers in the frame, so the square's signature sign reads clearly in one shot. The square itself lies to the south of you, so the letters, the maguey and the groups of mariachis fall into one view.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the letters up with a horizontal grid line so they sit level. Include a few musicians or passers-by for scale and life, and avoid cutting the end letters off. If you want a calmer alternative, try the quieter Callejón de la Amargura, an older-looking alley nearby.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the letters to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so bright signs and lights don't wash out in the evening. In low light, try night mode and hold the phone steady against your body. Moving musicians may blur, so take a few shots.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: The square is liveliest in the evening, and Friday or Saturday night from 11:00 p.m. is a good choice for the full atmosphere. For a calmer shot with fewer people in front of the letters, visit in daylight.

text.access_note: This is an open public square, but the surrounding area has a reputation for petty crime, so keep valuables close; check the official site before you go for anything ticketed nearby, such as the Museo del Tequila y el Mezcal.

name: Zócalo
label: Zócalo
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Catedral Metropolitana' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Catedral Metropolitana de la Ciudad de México' (way/862852010): middle (166 m across); moved 30 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/19430125: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Constitution Square' (235 m across).
notes: The vast main square of the historic centre.

text.description:
The Zócalo is the main square of Mexico City, formally called Plaza de la Constitución. It measures about 240 m by 240 m and is lined with big, solid buildings: the Metropolitan Cathedral on the north side, the National Palace to the east and city government buildings to the south. In the middle stands a flagpole with an enormous Mexican flag, which is raised and lowered every day. Long before the Spanish arrived, this was the heart of the Aztec city of Tenochtitlan, and the Templo Mayor site is just a block to the northeast. The name means 'plinth': a column was planned as a monument to independence, but only the base was ever built.

For a phone photo, a single-building view works well. From the front of the cathedral you can fill the frame with its ornate facade, tile patterns and carved doors, with the open plaza spreading out in front. It is calmer than trying to squeeze the whole square into one shot. The cathedral was built in the latter half of the 16th century, and its three portals face south over the plaza, which is why the square still has a north–south feel today. The square often hosts large events, such as exhibitions and temporary arenas, which can block your view, so be ready to shift a few steps to find a clear line.
text.geographic_location: The Zócalo is the main square in the historic centre of Mexico City. It sits one block southwest of the Templo Mayor site, with the Metropolitan Cathedral on its north edge and the National Palace on its east side.
text.directions_text: Head for the Centro Histórico, the historic centre of Mexico City. If you come by metro, the Zócalo/Tenochtitlan station has an entrance at the northeast corner of the square, but no sign above ground shows it. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole cathedral facade with some plaza in front. Switch to the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the carved doors and tile patterns. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want the facade and a big sweep of open square together.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Catedral Metropolitana (from the plaza, facing the main facade on the north edge of the Zócalo). The cathedral's ornate facade and tiled patterns in the foreground, with the plaza opening out in front of it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the facade square to the frame so the vertical lines stay straight. Tilt the phone up only a little, or the towers will lean inwards. Leave a strip of open plaza at the bottom for scale. For a wider alternative, walk out into the square and photograph the giant flag in the middle, framed by the cathedral and the National Palace.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the facade to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a touch so the sky does not wash out the carved stonework. Take a few frames in case people walk through.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Check whether an event is setting up, as stages and arenas can block the view.

text.access_note: The square is an open public space, but events can block parts of the view, so check before you go. The cathedral is a place of worship, so check the official site before you go if you want to go inside.
claims_not_in_sources: The cathedral facade faces south over the plaza, so it tends to catch daylight through much of the day.
A tilted-up phone makes tall towers appear to lean inwards.

name: National Museum of Anthropology
label: Museo de Antropología
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'El Paraguas' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'El Paraguas' (relation/17310243): middle (113 m across); moved 20 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/433756023: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Museo Nacional de Antropología' (378 m across).
notes: Home of the Aztec Sun Stone replica halls and the great umbrella fountain.

text.description:
The National Museum of Anthropology is the largest and most visited museum in Mexico, with 3.7 million visitors in 2024. It stands in Chapultepec Park and opened in 1964. Its architects, Pedro Ramírez Vázquez, Jorge Campuzano and Rafael Mijares Alcérreca, built the exhibition halls around a big central courtyard. The best-known feature there is El Paraguas, 'the umbrella': a huge square concrete canopy held up by one slender pillar, with a large reflecting pool in the courtyard. Water falls around the column, so the scene has movement as well as strong shapes.

It photographs well because everything lines up: the canopy overhead, the carved column, the reflecting pool and the visitors walking beneath. These give you a sense of scale. The museum has 23 exhibition rooms and covers almost 8 hectares, so the courtyard is a calm centre in a very large building. Outside, the gardens around the halls hold outdoor exhibits, including the Olmec colossal heads.

For a phone, this is an easy place to get a striking picture. Stand under the canopy, include a little of the pool and a few people, and keep the column upright in the frame. Flash is not allowed, and tripods should be treated as banned, so hold the phone steady with both hands and rest your elbows against your body. The courtyard is inside the museum, so check the official site before you go for tickets, hours and photography rules.
text.geographic_location: The museum is inside Chapultepec Park in Mexico City, in the area between Paseo de la Reforma and Mahatma Gandhi Street. Its entrance faces Paseo de la Reforma.
text.directions_text: Head for Chapultepec Park and the museum's entrance on the Paseo de la Reforma side. Once inside the entrance, walk straight into the central courtyard, where El Paraguas stands. Check the official site for how to enter and when. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole canopy, the column and the pool into one frame. Use the default lens (1x) for a calmer, more natural view. Try telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for the carved details on the column.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (central courtyard, under the canopy, just inside the entrance). The cantilevered umbrella canopy on its single column, with water falling around it and the reflecting pool and visitors in the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the column up with a vertical line so it stands straight. Leave some of the pool and a few people in the lower part of the picture to show scale. For a second view, a free option is Paseo de la Reforma, which shows the museum facade and entrance with the park trees around it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Switch flash off, as it is not allowed. Tap on the shaded underside of the canopy to focus, then nudge the exposure slider down if the bright sky is washing out. A Live Photo can capture the falling water, and you can pick the best frame afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon light suits garden photos. Check the official site for current hours before you go.

text.access_note: The courtyard is inside the museum and needs a paid ticket; photography is allowed without flash and tripods should be treated as banned, so check the official site before you go.

name: Palacio de Bellas Artes
label: Palacio de Bellas Arte
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Alameda Central' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Alameda Central' (way/4758957): middle (539 m across); moved 10 m off water.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/157051087: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Palacio de Bellas Artes' (137 m across).
notes: Marble opera house and arts palace.

text.description: The Palacio de Bellas Artes is Mexico City's great marble-clad opera house and arts centre, sometimes called the "art cathedral of Mexico". It photographs well because the pale facade and the golden dome stand out against the trees and sky of the Alameda Central park beside it. Work began in 1904 under the Italian architect Adamo Boari, but the heavy building sank into the soft ground and the Revolution stopped construction in 1913. It was finished under Federico Mariscal and opened on 29 November 1934. The exterior is mostly Art Nouveau and Neoclassical, with white marble on the facades, and the main front faces Avenida Juárez. Look out for the four Pegasus sculptures on the plaza side, which add interest to a close-up. For a calm, free, street-level view, walk into the Alameda and use the park's trees as a natural frame around the dome and facade. For a higher, wider view there is a café in the Sears building nearby, though you may have to buy something to get a window seat and there can be a long wait. Up close, the building is too large to fit in one frame without stepping back, so use the width of the park to your advantage.
text.geographic_location: The palace is on the western side of the historic centre of Mexico City, right beside the Alameda Central park. The Palacio de Correos (the old post palace) is across the street.
text.directions_text: Head for the Alameda Central on the western edge of the historic centre. From there the palace is to the east, about 5 minutes on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) so the trees, facade and dome all sit in the frame. Then try 2x to bring the dome closer and make it fill more of the picture. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) only when you are right beside the building and cannot step back.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Alameda Central (main east-west path inside the park, roughly at the midpoint, looking toward the dome). The facade and dome framed by the tree line as a foreground, a free alternative to the elevated view. From here the palace is straight ahead to the east. The facade and dome sit behind a line of trees that frame them.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Let the branches and tree line form a natural frame along the top and sides, and keep the dome near the centre. Switch on gridlines and line the path up with the middle of the frame so it leads the eye to the palace. For a different angle, you could try the elevated view from the Sears café nearby, or step closer to the building for a straight-on shot of the front.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the white marble on the screen to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the facade keeps its detail rather than turning bright white. If you want a wider scene with trees on both sides, try a panorama, moving slowly.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, when the facade catches direct light.

text.access_note: The Alameda Central is an open public park, but access to the palace's interior, exhibitions and performances, and any use of professional equipment outside, may be restricted or ticketed, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The Alameda Central is an open public park that anyone can walk into.
A phone's ultra-wide lens (0.5x) is useful when you are too close to fit a large building into the frame.
Sliding the exposure down on a phone helps keep detail in bright white marble.
The palace's interior and performances may be ticketed.

name: Chapultepec Castle
label: Chapultepec Castle
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Castillo de Chapultepec' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Museo Nacional de Historia Castillo de Chapultepec' (relation/17314437): middle (204 m across); moved 20 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/17314437: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Museo Nacional de Historia Castillo de Chapultepec' (204 m across).

text.description: Chapultepec Castle stands on top of Chapultepec Hill, at the entrance to Chapultepec park, about 2,325 metres above sea level. From the terrace you get a view over the city. The building began in 1785 as a stately home for a Spanish viceroy. It later became a military academy, then the home of Emperor Maximilian and Empress Carlota, and then a presidential residence. It has been the National Museum of History since 1939. Maximilian also ordered the straight boulevard that links the castle with the city centre. It was first called Paseo de la Emperatriz and is now Paseo de la Reforma. The best-known photo is that boulevard seen from the castle's east terrace. Guides call it the classic postcard shot, and one says it is among the few places where all of Reforma fits in a single frame. You see the avenue running away from you, with the skyline and the monuments in the traffic circles behind it. Morning is the time to aim for. Stay on the terrace for the view, but spend a minute on the castle itself too. Its exterior looks good framed by the gardens, with the city beyond. For a different picture, go to the Monumento a los Niños Héroes near the foot of the hill. From there you can shoot upwards at the castle's full profile against the sky. Entry to the terraces is through the museum, so plan your visit around that.
text.geographic_location: Chapultepec Castle is on top of Chapultepec Hill, at the entrance to Chapultepec park in Mexico City. Paseo de la Reforma runs from its foot towards the city centre.
text.directions_text: There are no Metro or tram stops listed for this spot, so head for Chapultepec park and make for the castle on the hill. The Monumento a los Niños Héroes near the foot of the hill is a handy landmark on the way. The east terrace facing Reforma is the recommended viewpoint. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole length of Reforma in one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a tidier view of the skyline. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the monuments in the traffic circles.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Castillo de Chapultepec (east terrace, facing Paseo de la Reforma). The boulevard Reforma running from the castle toward the city centre, with the skyline and traffic-circle monuments behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the boulevard along the middle line so it runs straight away from you. Keep the horizon level and leave some sky above the skyline. For an alternative, try the Monumento a los Niños Héroes near the foot of the hill, shooting upwards for the castle's full profile against the sky.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the boulevard to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky does not wash out. The checkered balcony is very bright, so check it is not overexposed. Keep flash off inside the museum.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning. Guides say afternoon light washes out the boulevard.

text.access_note: The terraces and gardens are reached through paid museum entry, so check the official site before you go for current days, hours and ticket rules.

name: Museo Soumaya
label: Museo Soumaya
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Plaza Carso' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Plaza Carso' (way/697923500): middle (410 m across); moved 15 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q2097646: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Silver hexagon-tiled museum in Plaza Carso.

text.description: The Museo Soumaya in Nuevo Polanco is a tall, curved building with no ordinary windows, covered in 16,000 hexagonal aluminium tiles. It stands 46 metres high on six floors and opened to the public in 2011. The architect was Fernando Romero. It forms one sculptural shape that changes with the light, which is why it works so well on a phone. The best photo is of the whole building, and for that you need to stand back. The open plaza in front of the entrance gives you the room. From there the curves and the tile pattern read as a single form instead of a wall of metal. Late in the day the tiles turn a warm amber-gold on the facade you can see. Once you have the full view, move closer and fill the frame with the hexagon pattern, which makes a good abstract shot. If you have time, the neighbouring Museo Jumex offers a higher, angled view of the facade across the plaza. Check whether its terrace needs a ticket before you plan around it. The building is part of the large Plaza Carso development, so expect other buildings and people at the edges of your frame. Wait a moment for a clear gap, or use them to show the scale.
text.geographic_location: The museum is in Nuevo Polanco, in the north of Mexico City, inside the large Plaza Carso development. The Museo Jumex is next door.
text.directions_text: Head for the Plaza Carso development in Nuevo Polanco and ask for the Museo Soumaya. From there the building is to the south-west, about 2 minutes on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the full facade from the plaza. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you cannot step back far enough. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for close shots of the tile pattern.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Plaza Carso (open plaza in front of the museum entrance, west-facing side for late light). The full curved, hexagon-tiled facade from a distance, which guides say needs room to read as a form. The museum lies to the south-west of you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the building centred, so the vertical lines stay straight. Step back until the whole shape fits with some sky around it. Then take a second shot using the telephoto to fill the frame with tiles. For a different angle, the Museo Jumex terrace looks across the plaza at the facade from higher up.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the bright part of the facade to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the shiny tiles keep their detail and colour. Take a few shots, because moving people and passing clouds change the picture.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon, or the 30 minutes before sunset, when the tiles turn amber-gold.

text.access_note: The plaza outside is open public space. Access to the Museo Jumex terrace is unconfirmed and may be ticketed or restricted, so check the official site before you go. Check the museum's official site for current opening times too.
claims_not_in_sources: Shiny metal tiles can reflect bright light, so lowering the exposure slider helps keep detail.
Other buildings and people in the Plaza Carso development may appear at the edges of photos taken from the plaza.
Gridlines help keep the building's vertical lines straight in a phone photo.

name: Templo Mayor
label: Templo Mayor
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'El Mayor' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'El Mayor' (node/4166517292): point; moved 5 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from the Wikipedia article 'Templo Mayor'.
notes: Aztec temple ruins beside the cathedral.

text.description: The Templo Mayor was the main temple of the Mexica people in their capital, Tenōchtitlan, which is now Mexico City. It was dedicated to Huītzilōpōchtli, god of war, and Tlāloc, god of rain and agriculture. At its base it measured roughly 100 by 80 metres. Building began sometime after 1325, and the temple was rebuilt six times, each stage over the one before. The Spanish destroyed it in 1521, and it was only fully excavated from 1978 after workers found a huge carved stone disk of the goddess Coyolxauhqui. Today you see the stone platforms, staircases and serpent-head sculptures, with the Metropolitan Cathedral nearby. The El Mayor restaurant terrace gives an elevated view over the excavations. It is a quieter option than the ground-level shots, and it lets you show the layers of stonework and how the ruins sit among the Centro Histórico buildings. The ruins themselves have almost no shade, so a visit early in the morning is more comfortable. Take the wide view from the terrace first. If you go into the site, you can then get closer to the carved details.
text.geographic_location: The Templo Mayor is in the Centro Histórico of Mexico City, in the block between Seminario and Justo Sierra streets, just north-east of the Zócalo. The terrace is at República de Argentina 15, on the corner of Justo Sierra.
text.directions_text: No station is listed for this spot. The Zócalo, the main plaza, lies south-west of the temple site. From the Zócalo, head north-east towards Justo Sierra and República de Argentina. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the whole excavated area from above. Use the default lens (1x) for a cleaner, less stretched view. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the stone platforms and sculptures.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on El Mayor (restaurant terrace at República de Argentina 15, corner of Justo Sierra). A view down onto the Templo Mayor excavations from above street level. From here you look down onto the Templo Mayor excavations from above street level, with the ruins lying to the south-west.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on your phone's gridlines and place the ruins in the lower two-thirds, so the layers of stone stay the main subject. Include a little of the surrounding Centro Histórico buildings for scale. For a different angle, the street-level view from Seminario shows the ruins and the adjacent museum framed by the old buildings. Inside the site, the serpent-head platforms in the foreground with the cathedral towers behind make a good shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stonework to set focus and exposure, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the pale stone looks washed out. Check the screen for reflections before you shoot if you are shooting through any glass.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, because the ruins have almost no shade.

text.access_note: The ruins are a ticketed site, so check the official site before you go; photography without flash is allowed but tripods are not, and the El Mayor terrace is a restaurant where you are expected to order something.

name: Angel of Independence
label: Angel of Independence
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Paseo de la Reforma' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Paseo de la Reforma nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/1420845680: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Angel of Independence' (48 m across).
notes: Golden victory column on Paseo de la Reforma.

text.description:
The Angel of Independence, officially the Monumento a la Independencia, is a victory column standing on a roundabout on Paseo de la Reforma. It was finished in 1910 for the centenary of the start of Mexico's War of Independence, to a design by Antonio Rivas Mercado. The column is 36 metres high. At the top is a 6.7-metre bronze figure of Nike, covered in 24k gold and restored in 2006. Below it, the base carries bronze sculptures and a lion guiding a child, and a mausoleum for independence heroes lies beneath.

It photographs well because the gold figure stands out against the sky and the long, straight avenue gives you a ready-made frame. From there you can place the column against the avenue and its modern towers, which gives a good 'city meets monument' picture. This side is also a little less crowded than the base.

Take care with traffic, as the roundabout is busy. Cross only at crosswalks and when the lights allow. Fencing or renovation boarding has been reported around the base, which can block close shots. Reforma is closed to cars on Sunday mornings for cycling and walking, which makes shooting easier.
text.geographic_location: The monument stands on a roundabout on Paseo de la Reforma, the major avenue running through downtown Mexico City. Modern towers line the avenue behind it.
text.directions_text: Head for the roundabout on Paseo de la Reforma in downtown Mexico City. Once there, use the crosswalks to reach the median strip on the Chapultepec side of the avenue, and stand there with the monument in front of you. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the column with the avenue stretching behind it. Switch to the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pull the towers closer to the column. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you are close and want the whole column in the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Paseo de la Reforma (median strip (camellón) on the side facing Chapultepec). The column framed against the long avenue and its modern towers, the classic 'city meets monument' composition. Look east to the column. Do not step into the traffic lanes.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the column on one of the vertical lines, so the avenue leads the eye towards it. Keep the gold figure clear of the buildings behind it. For a closer, front-on view of the base and the Angel with fewer vehicles in the frame, try the Monumento a la Independencia side. For a wider view with the avenue's skyline behind it, go along Paseo de la Reforma.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the column to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the sky stays blue and the gold keeps its detail. At night, use night mode and brace your elbows against your body or a solid surface to keep the phone steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: At night, when the column is lit up. A Sunday morning also works well, because Reforma is closed to cars and the median and base are easier to shoot.

text.access_note: The roundabout and median are open public space, but access to the base and the interior climb is not reliable, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The monument is lit at night, and night mode can cope with that lighting.
A telephoto lens (2x-5x) makes distant towers look closer to the column.
Lowering the exposure slider helps keep sky and gold detail.

name: National Palace
label: National Palace
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Plaza de la Constitución' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Plaza de la Constitución' (relation/19430125): middle (235 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/6191295: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'National Palace' (308 m across).
notes: Government seat with Diego Rivera murals.

text.description: The National Palace fills the whole eastern side of Mexico City's main square, the Zócalo, and its long red tezontle facade is the reason to come. It runs for more than 200 metres, with a tower at each end and three big doorways in between. Above the central doorway is the balcony where the president gives the Grito on the evening of 15 September, just before 11pm, and rings the bell that Father Miguel Hidalgo used to call for rebellion. The site has been a seat of power since the Aztec ruler Moctezuma II had his "New Houses" here, and some of that older building material was reused. The palace is also the president's official residence, and inside are Diego Rivera's murals. From the square, your job is simple: show how long the building is, with open space in front of it. Stand on the west side and look east so the whole front fits, then step in for a second shot of the central balcony and bell. The square is big and open, so there is no clever angle. A straight-on, level shot works best. The square is often used for events and has had a temporary ice rink, which can block the classic view. If you can, also walk round to the palace's quieter back side, with its garden and courtyard setting, for a calmer picture.
text.geographic_location: In the historic centre of Mexico City, on the east side of the Zócalo (Plaza de la Constitución), the city's main square. The palace fills the whole side of the square.
text.directions_text: No Metro or tram stop is listed for this spot, so walk or use local transport to the Zócalo in the historic centre and head onto the square. From there the palace is straight ahead to the east, about 220 m away, roughly 3 minutes on foot across the open square. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) held in landscape to take in the whole facade. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the square and sky, or if people crowd the edges. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the central balcony, the bell niche and the two towers.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Plaza de la Constitución (west side of the square, facing east toward the palace's long facade). The full length of the palace's Zócalo-facing facade, with the plaza and its open space in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the roofline up with a horizontal line so the long facade doesn't tilt. Keep the central balcony near the middle of the frame and leave a band of open square along the bottom. Hold the phone level, because tilting it makes the towers lean. If you have time, walk round to the palace's quieter back side for a second, calmer view with its garden and courtyard setting.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the palace to focus, then pull the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the red stone keeps its colour. Take a few shots in case people walk through the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, when guides say crowds are thinner. The facade faces the square, so it may get more direct light later in the day. Use the exposure slider if the sun is low behind the building.

text.access_note: The Zócalo is an open public square, but the palace is a working government building with only some parts open to visitors, so check the official site before you go, especially for interior access and photo rules.

name: Monument to the Revolution
label: Monumento a la Revoluc
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Plaza de la República' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Plaza de la República' (relation/7841259): middle (305 m across); moved 5 m off water.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/158032450: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Monumento a la Revolución' (57 m across).

text.description: The Monument to the Revolution is a huge stone arch topped by a copper dome, and it stands in the middle of Plaza de la República in downtown Mexico City. At 67 m it is the tallest triumphal arch in the world, so it fills a phone frame quickly. It began as a grand legislative palace under President Porfirio Díaz, with the first stone laid in 1910. The Revolution stopped the work, and the shell stood unfinished for about twenty-five years. In the 1930s it was turned into a monument with Art Deco touches and stone sculpture groups, finished in 1938. Several key figures of the Revolution are buried inside. The best-known picture is the straight-on view across the plaza. The fountains in the foreground give a sense of scale, and the open square means nothing blocks the view. People often play in the water, which adds life to the frame. Keep the phone level so the tall columns do not lean, and leave a little sky above the dome. If you want a quieter picture, try the monument seen down the side street Ignacio Ramírez, which is usually less busy than the plaza. There is also an observation deck with wide views over the city, but check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: In Plaza de la República in central Mexico City, near Paseo de la Reforma and Avenida de los Insurgentes.
text.directions_text: Head for central Mexico City, near Paseo de la Reforma and Avenida de los Insurgentes, by taxi or hired scooter. Ask to be dropped at Plaza de la República. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the whole arch with the fountains in front. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a cleaner view of the monument alone, and use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the dome, arches and stone sculptures.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Plaza de la República (across the plaza from the monument, with the fountains in the foreground). The full monument with its copper dome and arches, framed by the plaza's fountains and people playing in the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the columns up with the vertical lines so the arch stands straight. Put the fountains in the lower third and the dome near the top, with a little sky above it. For a different angle, try the monument down the side street Ignacio Ramírez.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the monument to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky stays blue and the stone keeps its detail. Try a Live Photo when people are playing in the fountains, so the moving water is caught.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people in the plaza. Check the sky first, as the dome and stone show up best against blue or lightly clouded sky.

text.access_note: The plaza is an open public square. The observation deck is a paid entry, so check the official site before you go.

name: House of Tiles
label: Casa de los Azulejos
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Avenida Francisco I. Madero' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Francisco I. Madero' (node/10582818903): point.
pin_note: Position from OSM N2812606361 (The House of Tiles): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Baroque palace covered in blue tiles.

text.description:
The House of Tiles (Casa de los Azulejos) is a building at Madero 4 whose outer walls are covered in blue-and-white Talavera tiles. It is the main reason people stop here, and guides call it the most photographed building on this street. It photographs well because the pattern is bold and the colours are simple. The tiles also sit against the carved stone windows and balconies of the old palace, so even a quick phone picture has plenty of detail.

The best view is from the pedestrian street directly in front of the facade. Standing there lets you frame the whole front head-on from street level. You can also walk a little way along Avenida Francisco I. Madero and take the house at an angle, with the tiled wall running away towards the corner. That second view gives more depth and is a good alternative if the pavement is busy.

If you go inside, the tiled courtyard has arches and balconies, and there is a mural by Orozco on the upper staircase. The light there is dimmer. The courtyard is used as a restaurant space and the tables are often taken, so be considerate when taking photos. Go early if you can, because midday street crowds and vendors are heavy.
text.geographic_location: The House of Tiles is at Madero 4, on the pedestrian street Avenida Francisco I. Madero in central Mexico City.
text.directions_text: Head for the pedestrian stretch of Avenida Francisco I. Madero in the centre of Mexico City. Look for number 4, the building covered in blue-and-white tiles. Madero, about 94 m south-west of the house. Walk about 94 m north-east along the pedestrian street to reach the tiled facade at Madero 4. Confirm the approach along Madero on the ground, as street layouts and crowds can change. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the facade from the street. If the pavement is narrow and you cannot fit the whole front in, switch to ultra-wide (0.5x). Use 2x to pick out a patch of tiles or a balcony.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Avenida Francisco I. Madero (on the pedestrian street directly in front of the tiled facade (Madero 4)). The full blue-and-white Talavera facade, framed head-on from street level with the palace's carved stone windows and balconies visible.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the edges of the facade up with them so the building does not lean. Keep the phone level and take it head-on. For a second photo, walk along Madero and shoot the house at an angle, letting the tiled wall run towards the corner. In the courtyard, try the arches and balconies, and the Orozco mural on the upper staircase.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the tiles to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the blue and white stay crisp and the white does not wash out. Indoors, where it is dimmer, hold the phone steady and let night mode work if it switches on.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Before 9am, when the light hits the tiles cleanly and the street is quieter. Midday light is flat and the pavement gets crowded.

text.access_note: The facade can be photographed from the public pedestrian street, but the courtyard is a restaurant space, so check the official site before you go for interior access and photo rules.

name: Alameda Central
label: Alameda Central
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Hemiciclo a Juárez' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Hemiciclo a Juárez' (way/992941278): middle (36 m across); moved 5 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/4758957: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Alameda Central' (539 m across).
notes: Historic public park next to Bellas Artes.

text.description: Alameda Central is a leafy public park in the middle of downtown Mexico City, and it is the oldest public park in the Americas, laid out in 1592. Paved paths fan out in a starburst around fountains and statues, so there is always something to put in the foreground. The best-known sight is the Hemiciclo a Juárez, a large white semicircular monument to Benito Juárez on the Avenida Juárez side of the park. Its neoclassical white curve with gold and bronze details stands out against the green of the trees, and the park's 2012 renewal (new marble paving, new trees and tidied features) means it looks fresh and bright. From there you can look toward the Hemiciclo and start with the monument in a single frame, then wander into the park. Once you are in the park, two more pictures are worth looking for. One is a fountain's female figure holding a pitcher, with the Torre Latinoamericana rising behind. The other is the dome of the Palacio de Bellas Artes seen down a path, with the trees framing it. Keep the monument straight in the frame and let the trees form the edges. Wait a moment for people to move through, as the paths are busy with walkers.
text.geographic_location: In the Cuauhtémoc borough of downtown Mexico City, between Avenida Juárez and Avenida Hidalgo, right next to the Palacio de Bellas Artes.
text.directions_text: The park sits beside the Palacio de Bellas Artes and can be reached from Metro Bellas Artes. The Hemiciclo a Juárez is on the Avenida Juárez (south) side of the park, facing the street. If you are coming from elsewhere in the city, a taxi to the Bellas Artes area is the simplest way, then walk to the Avenida Juárez side. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the Hemiciclo so the curve and lines stay natural. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close and the whole curve will not fit. For the fountain figure with the tower behind it, try telephoto (2x or more) to bring the tower closer.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (southeast side, facing Avenida Juárez). The white neoclassical semicircular monument with its gold and bronze ornaments, framed by the park's trees.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the centre of the monument with the middle of the frame, keeping the trees as a border on each side. For a different shot, walk into the park for a fountain's female figure holding a pitcher with the Torre Latinoamericana behind, or look along a path to see the Bellas Artes dome framed by the tree line.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the white marble to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the white keeps its detail and the gold ornaments do not burn out. At dusk, let night mode work and hold the phone steady against a wall or railing.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or dusk, when the light is soft and the monument looks bright without harsh glare.

text.access_note: Alameda Central is a public park, but check the official site before you go in case of works or temporary closures.
claims_not_in_sources: Keeping the phone steady against a wall or railing helps with night mode shots.
The paths in the park can be busy with people walking through.
Dropping the exposure slider helps keep detail in white marble and gold ornaments in bright light.

name: Torre Latinoamericana
label: Torre Latinoamericana
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/6071992: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Torre Latinoamericana' (58 m across).
notes: Skyscraper with a viewing deck over the centre.

text.description:
The Torre Latinoamericana is a 166 m skyscraper in downtown Mexico City, and one of the city's best-known landmarks. It opened on 30 April 1956 and was Mexico's tallest completed building for almost 27 years, until 1982. Its reputation rests on how it handles earthquakes. It came through the big 1985 quake without damage, while several other buildings nearby were harmed, and many locals see it as a symbol of safety. For a phone photographer that story gives you a good reason to stop and look up. It is a tall, slim steel-framed tower, and it stands out clearly against the older buildings around it.

There are two ways to photograph it. From the street, point the phone upwards and let the tower's height fill the frame. Or go up to the public observation deck on the 44th floor, the highest in Mexico City, and photograph the city spread out around you. Check the official site before you go to confirm access and tickets. The tower is also a nice detail in wider street scenes, so take a few steps back whenever you can and use the buildings around it as a frame. Keep the phone level so the tower does not lean.
text.geographic_location: The tower stands in downtown Mexico City, in the city's central area, where it rises well above the buildings around it.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for downtown Mexico City and use a map app to navigate to the Torre Latinoamericana. The phone icon on the map is at the tower itself, in the middle of its outline, so head to the tower and shoot upwards from its base. Step back across the street to try different angles and fit in the whole building. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole tower in from close up. Switch to the default lens (1x) for natural-looking views and to the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details of the upper floors.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Head to the tower and shoot upwards from its base. For a view of the whole tower, step back to the far side of the street. If you go up to the 44th floor observation deck, you can photograph the city from there; check the official site before you go.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the tower up with a vertical line so it does not lean. With the ultra-wide, keep the tower in the centre of the frame to limit stretching at the edges. Add a bit of street or nearby buildings at the bottom of the shot for scale. From the deck, press the phone close to the glass, if there is any, to cut reflections.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the sky or the tower to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky does not turn white. At dusk, try night mode and brace your elbows against something steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Pick a clear day, as haze or cloud will flatten the view from the deck. Late afternoon into dusk suits both the tower and the city lights.

text.access_note: The tower is a working office building with a public observation deck on the 44th floor, so check the official site before you go for access and tickets.

name: Mexico City Metropolitan Cathedral
label: Metropolitan Cathedral
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Plaza de la Constitución' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Plaza de la Constitución' (relation/19430125): middle (235 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/862852010: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Catedral Metropolitana de la Ciudad de México' (167 m across).
notes: Largest cathedral in the Americas, on the Zócalo.

text.description:
Mexico City's cathedral stands on the northern side of the Zócalo, the Plaza de la Constitución. It took just under 250 years to build, from 1573 to 1813, so the stonework mixes Gothic, Baroque, Churrigueresque and Neoclassical styles. It stands on the old Aztec sacred precinct, close to the Templo Mayor. The building is about 59 metres wide and 67 metres to the tips of its two bell towers, with a central dome and three main portals.

It photographs well because the plaza gives you room to step back. From the middle of the square the full stone front fits in one picture, with both towers, the main entrance and the giant flag pole. A lone figure in the foreground shows how big the place is. The front faces south, towards the square.

Go early if you can. Morning light is warmer on the stone and there are fewer people in your frame. The Zócalo is also used for public events, and stages or crowds can block the view, so look at the square before you plan your shot. For a different angle, try Calle Madero, where the buildings on either side frame the cathedral's front from further back. Both viewpoints are at street level and are free to use.
text.geographic_location: In the historic centre of Mexico City, on the northern side of the Plaza de la Constitución (the Zócalo), next to the Templo Mayor site.
text.directions_text: Head for the historic centre and the Plaza de la Constitución (Zócalo). From there the cathedral is about 3 minutes on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close or want the whole front and some sky in one frame. From further back, the default lens (1x) gives a more natural look. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as a bell tower or the carved portals.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Plaza de la Constitución (middle of the plaza, facing north toward the cathedral facade). The full stone facade with both bell towers and the main entrance, framed by the open plaza and the giant flag pole.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Step back as far as the plaza allows so the whole front fits. Turn on the gridlines and line the towers up with the vertical lines, holding the phone level so the towers don't lean. Add a person or two in the foreground for scale. If the square is blocked by an event, try Calle Madero for a street-level view of the front framed by the buildings.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the facade to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the stone keeps its detail. Take a few shots at slightly different zoom levels and pick the best later.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or sunrise, when the facade is lit in golden light and there are fewer people.

text.access_note: The plaza and the street views are open public space, but the Zócalo can be closed off or crowded during events; inside the cathedral photography is restricted (no flash, no tripods, no photos in some areas such as the crypt), so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The ultra-wide lens can fit the whole facade in from closer up, but it may stretch the edges of the frame.
Tilting the phone upward makes the towers appear to lean inwards, so holding it level and using gridlines helps.
Stages or crowds for public events in the Zócalo can block the view of the cathedral.

name: Palacio Postal
label: Palacio Postal
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Palacio Postal' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OSM W157051114 (Palacio Postal): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.

text.description: The Palacio Postal is a grand building where the best photograph is inside. Step into the main hall and look up: the atrium rises through stacked galleries of gilded ironwork under an ornate ceiling. It is the part of the building people photograph most, and it suits a phone well because everything is lined up for a straight-up view. The most dramatic result comes from the centre of the ground floor, pointing the phone upward so the galleries seem to climb away from you. The grand staircase and the ceiling make good second pictures. If you can get to the upper level, a downward shot of the staircase and the hall below gives a very different view, though that depends on which areas are open on the day. From outside, the pale, ornate facade and main entrance look best from the street corner where Eje Central Lázaro Cárdenas meets Calle de Tacuba. That makes a simple opening shot before you go in. Interiors can be dim and the gold catches the light, so take a moment to tap and adjust the exposure before pressing the shutter. Avoid flash, and follow any signs about photography. Entry to the interior may be ticketed or restricted, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: The Palacio Postal is in Mexico City. The corner where Eje Central Lázaro Cárdenas meets Calle de Tacuba is a good place to view its facade from.
text.directions_text: No Metro or tram stop is listed for this spot, so use the corner of Eje Central Lázaro Cárdenas and Calle de Tacuba as your reference point. The facade and main entrance can be seen from that corner. Once you are inside, the phone icon on the map is in the middle of the ground-floor hall, so there is no further walk. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) inside, so the atrium and galleries fit in one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for the staircase or for details of the ironwork. Telephoto (2x-5x) is useful for picking out ceiling detail from the floor.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. This shows the stacked gilded ironwork and the ornate ceiling from the middle of the hall. For an alternative, shoot down from the upper level at the grand staircase and the hall below, if that area is open. From outside, the corner of Eje Central Lázaro Cárdenas and Calle de Tacuba shows the facade and main entrance.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and hold the phone level, then tilt it slowly upward so the vertical lines stay as straight as possible. Keep the galleries symmetrical on both sides of the frame. Include a little of the floor or a person for scale if the hall is quiet. The staircase and ceiling make good second frames.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Leave the flash off. Tap on a mid-bright area of the ironwork to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the gold keeps its detail. Hold your elbows against your body to keep the phone steady in the dim light, and use night mode only if the image looks dark and you can stay still.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Visit when the building is open and the hall is quieter, so you get a clear view of the floor.

text.access_note: Access to the interior may be ticketed or restricted, so check the official site before you go.

name: National Museum of Art
label: Museo Nacional de Arte
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Plaza Manuel Tolsá' (5 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Plaza Manuel Tolsá' (way/30724753): middle (119 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/14592229: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Museo Nacional de Arte' (113 m across).

text.description:
The National Museum of Art, known as MUNAL, sits on Tacuba in the historic centre of Mexico City. It is a big, pale, ornate building, and it photographs well because of the square in front of it. Manuel Tolsá's bronze equestrian statue of Charles IV, nicknamed El Caballito, stands in the plaza that carries Tolsá's name. It gives you a strong foreground shape against the facade, so one frame shows both the building and the statue.

The building was designed by the Italian architect Silvio Contri as the Palace of Communications, built to show Mexico's commitment to modernisation. Its style mixes several earlier styles, and the decorative details were made by the Coppedé family of Florence. It has been an art museum since 1982, was restored and re-opened in 2000, and holds more than 3,000 works of Mexican art. The statue has stood in its present spot since 1979.

For your photo, stand in the plaza in front of the statue and look north toward the main facade. Keep the horse and rider on one side of the frame so they don't hide the museum's entrance. Leave a little sky above the roofline, and use the gridlines to keep the building's vertical edges straight. Take a second shot a little closer with the statue larger and the facade softer behind it, which makes a good postcard-style picture.
text.geographic_location: MUNAL is in the Centro Histórico of Mexico City, at Tacuba 8. It faces Plaza Manuel Tolsá, where El Caballito stands.
text.directions_text: There are no Metro or tram stops listed for this spot, so start from the Centro Histórico, the historic centre of Mexico City, and head for Tacuba street and Plaza Manuel Tolsá. If you are coming from further away, head for Tacuba 8 in the Centro Histórico and then walk to Plaza Manuel Tolsá. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole facade and the statue together, then switch to the default lens (1x) for a cleaner, less stretched view. If you want a close shot of the statue or the facade's details, use the telephoto/zoom (2x-5x, depending on your phone).
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Plaza Manuel Tolsá (In the plaza in front of the equestrian statue, looking north toward the main facade). The museum's white neoclassical main facade framed behind the bronze equestrian statue 'El Caballito' in the foreground. The facade is only a short walk away, so you don't need to go any further back.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the facade up with them so the building stands straight. Put the statue off-centre, either left or right, and let the facade fill the background. For a closer variation, use the telephoto/zoom (2x-5x) and frame the horse and rider with the entrance behind them.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the facade to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the white stonework looks too bright or washed out. If the bronze statue goes too dark against the pale building, tap on the statue instead and then lower the exposure slightly.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and gentler shadows on the facade than the middle of the day.

text.access_note: The plaza is an open-air public square, but the museum itself may have ticketing and photography rules, so check the official site before you go.

name: Centro Coyoacán
label: Coyoacán centre
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Jardín Centenario' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Plaza Jardín Centenario' (way/54235991): middle (164 m across).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q431083: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Charming plazas, church and cafés of old Coyoacán.

text.description: The name Centro Coyoacán on this map points to a former shopping centre, but the photo to take is in the old heart of Coyoacán, at Jardín Centenario. Stand in front of the bronze Fuente de los Coyotes, in the middle of the garden. The fountain sits in the foreground, with the garden's trees and arches around it, which gives a classic postcard picture. Guides name it as the most photographed spot in Coyoacán. For a second picture, Jardín Hidalgo is just across the way. It has a 19th-century kiosco with a stained-glass cupola and a bronze eagle, and the historic town hall building stands behind it. A little history explains the map name. The Centro Coyoacán mall stood on Av. Coyoacán and Av. Universidad and opened in 1989 as the first mall of El Palacio de Hierro, designed by Javier Sordo Madaleno. It closed on 19 September 2022, and its site is being absorbed into the neighbouring Mítikah complex. For photos, keep the fountain central and let the trees and arches fill the edges. Early morning light is attractive, and the fountain is attractive when lit at night. The kiosco was being restored when one visitor went, so scaffolding may hide it. Check before you go.
text.geographic_location: The historic centre of Coyoacán, in Mexico City, where Jardín Centenario and Jardín Hidalgo face each other. The former Centro Coyoacán mall site lies to the north-west, by Av. Coyoacán and Av. Universidad.
text.directions_text: No Metro or tram stop is listed for this spot, so navigate to Jardín Centenario on the map. The former Centro Coyoacán mall site is to the north-west of it, about 1.3 km away. Jardín Hidalgo is a short walk across from the fountain. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the fountain with the trees and arches around it. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the fountain fills too little of the frame or the crowd gets in the way. Use telephoto (2x or more) for details of the Jardín Hidalgo kiosco from a distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Jardín Centenario (in front of the coyote fountain, at the centre of the garden). The bronze Fuente de los Coyotes in the foreground with the garden's trees and arches around it, framed for a classic postcard image.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the fountain on the centre line, with the trees and arches filling the sides. Hold the phone level so the arches stay straight. For a second shot, walk across to Jardín Hidalgo and photograph the kiosco with the town hall building behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the fountain to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the bronze keeps its detail against the bright sky. At night, use night mode and hold still for the second or two it takes.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, or night when the fountain is lit.

text.access_note: Jardín Centenario and Jardín Hidalgo are open public plazas; check before you go, as the Jardín Hidalgo kiosco may be under restoration.

name: Chapultepec
label: Bosque de Chapultepec
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Castillo de Chapultepec' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q523194: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Huge city park with lake and museums.

text.description:
Chapultepec is Mexico City's great green lung: a forest park of just over 866 hectares, centred on a rocky rise called Chapultepec Hill. The name comes from Nahuatl and means roughly 'at the grasshopper hill'. Aztec rulers used the hill as a retreat. In 1785 a castle was built on the summit, and it later became the home of Mexico's heads of state. It is also where, in 1847, the young cadets known as the Niños Héroes made their stand. The first section of the park is the oldest and busiest, and it is estimated to receive around 24 million visitors a year.

For photos, a quieter, less-photographed spot is the south garden terrace of the castle, an alternative to the classic east terrace. From here you look over the park lake, with the forest around it and, on clear winter days, the volcanoes to the southeast. It is described as more atmospheric than the classic view. A phone handles it well, because the scene is mostly layers of water, trees and sky. Look for a foreground, such as a balustrade, a plant or a bit of the terrace, to give the picture depth. Wait for a gap between visitors if you want a clean frame. The castle grounds are ticketed, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: Chapultepec Park is a large forest park in the middle of Mexico City. The castle stands on Chapultepec Hill in the park's oldest, first section, close to the Museum of Anthropology and the zoo.
text.directions_text: Head for the castle on top of Chapultepec Hill, in the first section of Chapultepec Park, and check local transport options for getting there. The south garden terrace is within the castle grounds, which have paid entry. If the phone icon on the map looks to be away from the hill, trust the castle itself and use the map as a rough guide. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the terrace, the lake and the trees in one frame. Use the default lens (1x) for a more natural view. On a clear day, switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the volcanoes on the horizon.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Stand on the south garden terrace of Castillo de Chapultepec (paid entry), overlooking the park lake. From the terrace the lake sits in front of you, framed by the garden terrace and the forest, with the volcanoes to the southeast when the air is clear.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the lake on the lower third, with the treeline and sky above. Use part of the terrace as a foreground. For a second view, the castle grounds also give a look along Paseo de la Reforma towards the Angel of Independence and the downtown skyline, framed by the forest.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the lake or the far trees to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky keeps its colour. Wipe the lens before you shoot, as terraces and parks can be dusty.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Clear winter days give the best chance of seeing the volcanoes. Earlier in the day is often calmer on the terrace, but check the castle's opening times first.

text.access_note: The castle grounds are a museum site with ticketed entry, so check the official site before you go for tickets and opening times.

name: Paseo de la Reforma
label: Paseo de la Reforma
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Fuente de la Diana Cazadora' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Fuente de la Diana Cazadora' (way/1114974166): middle (43 m across); moved 15 m off water.
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q1478843: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Grand boulevard lined with monuments and towers.

text.description:
Paseo de la Reforma is a wide, tree-lined avenue that cuts diagonally across the middle of Mexico City. It was laid out in the 1860s under Emperor Maximilian, who wanted a grand European-style boulevard linking the city centre with Chapultepec Castle. It was first named after his wife, Empress Carlota, and was renamed Paseo de la Reforma in 1872. Today it is lined with hotels, offices and some of the city's tallest towers, and it is where parades and celebrations tend to gather.

For a phone photo, the best place to start is the fountain of Diana the Huntress, roughly midway along the avenue. From here you get the bronze statue and its water jets, framed by the broad road and the rows of trees. Guides describe it as a prime photo stop, and it is quieter than the Ángel de la Independencia roundabout. It looks especially good after dark, when the sculpture is lit. If you want the golden Ángel with the skyline behind it, that is the other classic view along the avenue.

Traffic is heavy, so keep to the pavements and the marked crossings. Most Sundays the main downtown stretch is closed to cars in the morning, which makes it the easiest time to take photos along the avenue. Keep the phone strap on your wrist and watch your surroundings while you frame the shot.
text.geographic_location: Paseo de la Reforma runs diagonally through the centre of Mexico City, from the historic centre towards Chapultepec Park. The Diana fountain stands roughly midway along it.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stop is listed for this spot, so go by taxi or ride-hailing and ask for the Fuente de la Diana Cazadora on Paseo de la Reforma, about halfway along the avenue. Chapultepec Park and Castle lie at the western end of the original Paseo. From the fountain, the old-centre end of the avenue lies to the north-east, about 2.3 km away in that direction. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to get the statue with the avenue and trees around it. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the avenue and the tree canopy. Try the telephoto (2x or more) for a tighter shot of the statue and its jets.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Fuente de la Diana Cazadora (midway along the avenue, shooting from the fountain's surroundings). The bronze Diana the Huntress statue with its water jets, framed by the wide avenue and the trees along it. Use the pavements and marked crossings rather than stepping into the road.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the statue on one of the lines, leaving the avenue and trees to lead the eye behind it. Keep the phone level so the tall buildings do not lean. For a different view, the golden Ángel de la Independencia, with the Reforma corridor and skyline behind it, is the alternative on the same avenue.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the statue to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the bright jets and sky do not wash out. After dark, use night mode and hold the phone against a wall or railing to keep it steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: At night, when the sculpture is lit. For fewer cars, try a Sunday morning, when the main downtown part of the avenue is usually closed to traffic.

text.access_note: This is an open public avenue and fountain area; there is no entry fee, but traffic is heavy, so check local conditions and Sunday closures before you go.
